text:
A US court found Google’s search business a monopoly because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act through exclusionary conduct, specifically by paying billions to secure default distribution deals [Source: ev-1]. Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that these payments—such as the approximately $26.3 billion spent in 2021 and the roughly 36% share of Safari search-ad revenue paid to Apple—created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generated scale, data, and quality that protected the dominant position against rivals [Source: ev-1].

The remedies ordered on August 5, 25 were structural and behavioral: Google is required to sell Chrome (the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000), it may no longer pay for default search placement or engage in revenue-sharing agreements, and it faces limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1].
